A feature release. The theme is voice, in both directions — you can now talk to
a session, and a session can talk back — plus the fixes that came out of
actually testing that on a Mac.

Still a beta, and two gaps are worth knowing before you read the rest: the
high-quality voice engine has **never been run on an Intel Mac** (only under
Rosetta on Apple silicon), and the eight British voices this release un-hides
have not been checked on Windows. Details under *Known limitations*.

## New: talk to a session

Turn on **Enable voice input** in Settings and hovering an orb fades in a small
mic badge. Click it, speak, click again (or wait 30 seconds) to stop. What you
said is transcribed **entirely on this machine** and typed into that session's
terminal.

**Enter is never pressed for you** — a misheard word is easy to fix or throw
away before it becomes a prompt.

Local is the point, not an afterthought: this has to work on a plain Claude
subscription rather than API billing, so nothing in the pipeline needs its own
account or a per-minute charge. Transcription is Whisper.net against a small
English-only model (`ggml-base.en`, about 150MB, downloaded once the first time
you enable it). Typing the result in reuses the exact terminal/tmux-pane
identification that click-to-focus already does, rather than inventing a second
way to find your pane.

## New: have a session read its answer back

The orb flyout gained a speaker button that reads the latest assistant turn
aloud. On macOS that uses Apple's Enhanced and Premium voices through `say`; on
Windows, the built-in voices — or either platform can use the new engine below.

## New: a genuinely good voice, on both platforms

**High-quality voice (experimental)** in Settings downloads a neural speech
engine and its model — about 300MB, once — and speaks entirely on this machine.
No cloud service, no API key, nothing leaves the computer.

It exists because Windows keeps its good voices locked inside Narrator, where no
third-party app can reach them; the best any app can otherwise get is
`Microsoft Zira Desktop`, which is over a decade old and sounds it. macOS gets it
too, even though Apple's voices are already decent, because some people prefer
Kokoro's and the engine turned out to be portable.

**This is the first release that actually ships the engine.** It is published as
its own asset per platform rather than bundled, so the installers stay the size
they were and anyone who never enables it pays nothing for it.

## New: bring your own voices, or your own engine entirely

Drop Kokoro `.npy` voice files into `ClaudeBuddy\voices` (`~/Library/Application
Support/ClaudeBuddy/voices` on macOS) and they appear in the picker beside the
bundled ones. That directory sits deliberately outside the engine's own folder,
which an upgrade replaces wholesale.

Or point the app at any command at all:

```jsonc
"speakCommand": "C:\\tools\\my-voice.cmd",
"speakCommandArgs": ["--voice", "whatever"]
```

Its voices appear in the **Speak voice** picker marked `(custom)`, alongside
`(system)` and `(Kokoro)` ones. Picking a voice is what selects the engine, so
all three are available at once rather than one hiding the others.

## New: eight British voices that were there all along

`bf_alice`, `bf_emma`, `bf_isabella`, `bf_lily`, `bm_daniel`, `bm_fable`,
`bm_george` and `bm_lewis` ship inside the engine bundle and were being filtered
out of the picker on both platforms — while the documentation told you `bf_`/`bm_`
were prefixes that would work. The bundled list goes from 20 voices to 28, and a
British voice you add yourself now shows up too.

## New: the orb flyout, tidied

Flyout buttons now sit in a semicircular arc rather than a flat row, there is a
settings button on it, and new orbs are absorbed into the active shape instead of
stacking up in a corner.

## Fixed: the macOS high-quality voice never made a sound

Enabling it on macOS turned the toggle on without giving it anything to play
through. The underlying library falls back to OpenAL off Windows, and that path
segfaults inside Apple's framework before a single sample is played — while the
app cheerfully reported that it was speaking, because the "now speaking" marker
fires before the audio device is even opened. The symptom was a pause, silence,
and then the whole turn again in the system voice.

macOS now synthesises and plays through `afplay`, which is the same
"speaking is a child process" shape the rest of the app already used — so
stopping still works, and stops immediately.

## Fixed: clicking an orb stopped crossing to another desktop

Click-to-focus kept working when the terminal was already on the desktop you
were looking at, and quietly did nothing when it wasn't. The script activated
the terminal, waited a fixed fifth of a second, then ordered the right window
front — and ordering a window front only pulls you to its Space once the app is
actually active. Measured on an idle machine, that activation took 145ms, 167ms
and 531ms on three consecutive runs: the average was inside the wait and the
spread was not, so roughly every third click lost the race and got quietly
undone. It now waits for the app to really be frontmost instead of guessing,
which is also slightly faster in the common case.

## Fixed, smaller

- The voice picker could show only a single voice, and the engine download could
  crash.
- An Intel Mac would have downloaded the Apple-silicon engine and been unable to
  run it; the download now follows the running process's architecture.
- The Windows hook recorded the wrong process as `session_pid` — the hook's
  parent rather than the real `claude` process.
- The `claude` CLI is now found by path instead of by asking a login shell,
  which was slow and broke on profiles that print things.

## Which file do I want

| Platform | Download |
| --- | --- |
| macOS, Apple silicon (M1 and later) | `ClaudeBuddy-0.3.0-beta-osx-arm64.dmg` |
| macOS, Intel | `ClaudeBuddy-0.3.0-beta-osx-x64.dmg` |
| Windows 10/11, 64-bit | `ClaudeBuddy-0.3.0-beta-win-x64-setup.exe` |

The `ClaudeBuddySpeech-0.3.0-beta-*.zip` assets are the optional high-quality
voice engine. **You do not download these yourself** — the app fetches the right
one when you turn the setting on. They are published here because that is where
it looks.

The .NET runtime is bundled; nothing else is needed. `SHA256SUMS.txt` covers
every file — verify with `shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS.txt` on macOS or
`Get-FileHash <file> -Algorithm SHA256` on Windows.

## Upgrading from 0.2.0-beta

**macOS**: replace the app in Applications. The signing identity is unchanged, so
your Automation permission carries over and click-to-focus keeps working. Hooks
are already wired; you don't need to run the hook installer again.

**Windows**: run the new setup over the old one. It upgrades in place, closing a
running copy if needed, and leaves your hook configuration alone.

Both voice features are **off by default** and download nothing until you turn
them on.

## Installing fresh

**macOS** — open the DMG, drag Claude Buddy to Applications, then double-click
**Install Claude Code Hooks.command**. Launch from Applications; nothing appears
in the Dock and no window opens, which is correct — look in the menu bar.

**Windows** — run the setup. Per-user, so no UAC prompt. Leave both checkboxes
ticked; tick **"Wire hooks for Claude Code running inside WSL"** too if you use
it.

### The hook step is not optional

Claude Buddy learns about your sessions from a hook Claude Code runs. Until it is
in `~/.claude/settings.json`, the app starts and runs correctly and shows
**nothing at all**. The installers offer to wire it up; let them. Existing
settings are backed up first, and re-running repairs rather than duplicating.

Hooks are read once at session start, so **restart any open Claude Code
sessions**.

## Known limitations

- **The high-quality voice engine has never run on a real Intel Mac.** It builds,
  signs and packs, and was exercised under Rosetta on Apple silicon — which runs
  the same x86-64 binary and the same libraries, but is not the same as native
  Intel hardware. If it fails there, it will fail by not starting, and the app
  falls back to the system voice rather than going silent.
- **The eight British voices have not been checked on Windows.** The fix is one
  shared call and changes the Windows picker too; only macOS was verified.
- **The high-quality voice was tested by driving the engine directly**, not
  through the app's own settings toggle and picker.
- **Voice dictation needs a permission you have to grant.** macOS asks for the
  microphone, and typing the text in needs Accessibility; if dictated text
  silently doesn't appear, that is the first place to look.
- **Windows installers are unsigned** — SmartScreen warns; choose **More info →
  Run anyway**. The macOS builds are signed and notarized, so they open normally.
- **WSL + tmux together isn't covered.**
- A session killed with Ctrl+C at a permission prompt can leave its orb stuck on
  amber. Right-click → *Reset this session to idle* clears it.

`docs/macos-neural-voice-findings.md` and `docs/windows-neural-voice-findings.md`
record what was measured and what is still assumed, if you want the long version.
